title: The Letter and the Spirit
goals: Express counterfactual conditions with formal precision: Were it not for, Had it not been for, But for, Should and Were to.
Master the complex passive structures used in legal and journalistic discourse (is alleged to have been, is being investigated, must be seen to be).
Express obligation, entitlement and responsibility with the exact preposition and modal (entitled to, liable for, bound by, notwithstanding).
Handle legal and ethical vocabulary: liability, precedent, accountable, impartial, whistleblower.
Negotiate and argue in formal contexts: setting conditions, conceding, rejecting and marking limits politely.
Write an argumentative text and a formal email with a mastery-level register and cohesion.

learn.title: Formal conditionals: Were it not for, Had it not been for, But for
learn.html:
In formal register (legal writing, reports, speeches) a condition is often expressed without if. These forms correspond to the Spanish “de no ser por…”, “de no haber sido por…” and “a no ser por…”, and all of them express a condition contrary to fact: something exists (or existed), so the hypothetical result does not happen.

FormulaReferenciaEjemploEquivalent with if
Were it not for + nounpresente / generalWere it not for the audit, the fraud would continue.If it weren't for the audit…
Had it not been for + nounpastHad it not been for her testimony, he would have been convicted.If it hadn't been for her testimony…
But for + nounpresent or past (the main verb tells you which)But for the appeal, he would be in prison. / But for the appeal, he would have served the full term.If it weren't / hadn't been for…
  • But for only takes a noun phrase (or a gerund with a subject: But for there being a loophole…, very formal); never a clause with a conjugated verb.
  • In inversion the negation is never contracted: Were it not for, not Weren't it for.
  • Other high-register conditional connectors: provided (that) / providing (that) / so long as / on condition that (restrictive, meaning “as long as”), unless (“unless”, = if … not), supposing / suppose / imagine (that) (hypothesis, often with a question in the main clause), in the event of / that (“in the event of”) and otherwise (“otherwise”).
  • Unless already contains the negation: you do not say unless … not. It is also not usually used in past counterfactual conditions, where if … not is more natural.

watch.wrong: If it wouldn't be for your testimony, he'd be convicted.
watch.right: Were it not for your testimony, he would be convicted.
watch.why: Never use would in the if-clause; the inversion Were it not for (or If it weren't for) expresses the idea of “if it weren't for”.

watch.wrong: Weren't it for the appeal, he would be in prison.
watch.right: Were it not for the appeal, he would be in prison.
watch.why: In formal inversion the negation is not contracted: Were it not for.

watch.wrong: But for the witness lied, the case would have collapsed.
watch.right: But for the witness's lie, the case would have collapsed.
watch.why: But for requires a noun phrase, not a clause with a conjugated verb.

watch.wrong: Unless you don't sign, the offer will expire.
watch.right: Unless you sign, the offer will expire.
watch.why: Unless already means if … not. In Spanish “a menos que no firmes” is fine, but in English the double negative is an error.

learn.title: Should, Were to and Had: inversion without if
learn.html:
The three auxiliaries can take the place of if and move in front of the subject. The result is more formal and more concise, typical of contracts, letters and official statements.

EstructuraSentidoEjemplo
Should + subject + base verba remote possibility; the main clause allows the imperative, will, mayShould you require further information, please contact our legal department.
Were + subject + to + base verban improbable or tentative hypothesis (future)Were the court to rule against us, we would appeal at once.
Had + subject + past participlean unreal past conditionHad we known about the clause, we would never have signed.
Were + subject + adjective/nounan unreal present condition with beWere the penalty proportionate, nobody would object.

Negativas: the particle not goes after the subject: Had they not disclosed the risks…; Should he not comply…. Contraction (Hadn't they…) is possible, but informal and unnatural in this register.

Matiz: If you should need help and Should you need help mean the same thing, but with should the speaker implies that the possibility is small and the offer is a courtesy. With were to it suggests that the situation is unlikely; If the court rules against us it presents it as a real possibility.

watch.wrong: Should you will need assistance, call us.
watch.right: Should you need assistance, call us.
watch.why: After Should + subject comes the base verb, without will.

watch.wrong: Were the court ruled against us, we would appeal.
watch.right: Were the court to rule against us, we would appeal.
watch.why: With future hypotheses: Were + subject + to + base verb.

watch.wrong: Had we not knew the risks, we would have refused.
watch.right: Had we not known the risks, we would have refused.

watch.wrong: Hadn't they disclosed the risks, the deal would have failed.
watch.right: Had they not disclosed the risks, the deal would have failed.
watch.why: In formal inversion not goes after the subject; the contracted form sounds colloquial and odd.

learn.title: Complex passives in legal and formal discourse
learn.html:
The passive is the central resource of formal English because it allows the agent to be omitted or backgrounded (when it is unknown, unimportant, or better left unnamed) and new information to be placed at the end. Beyond was built by, C2 requires mastery of these structures:

EstructuraEjemploNota
Verb of opinion/rumour + to be / to have beenThe defendant is alleged to have forged the signature.said, believed, thought, reported, alleged, known, understood, expected. To have been = an event prior to the moment of speaking.
Impersonal version with itIt is alleged that the company concealed the defects.Same information; more distance.
Continuous passiveThe documents are being examined. / The case was being heard when the verdict came.Ongoing process; is investigating by is being investigated is a frequent mistake.
Modal + be / have been + past participleJustice must not only be done but be seen to be done. / The clause ought to have been disclosed.Obligation, deduction and criticism in the passive.
Passive gerund: being / having been + past participleHe denies having been informed of his rights. She feared being sued.After prepositions and verbs such as deny, avoid, risk, resent.
Dos objetosThe claimant was awarded damages. / Damages were awarded to the claimant.Both objects can become the subject; the first is the more natural choice.
get-passiveTwo executives got fined. / He got sued for negligence.Informal; it usually implies an adverse or unexpected event.
Causative have / get + object + past participleWe had the contract reviewed by an independent lawyer.To arrange a service, or to suffer something: She had her licence revoked.

Watch out with suggest, propose, recommend, insist: they do not take a personal subject + to. One says It was suggested that he settle or It was recommended that the matter be referred to arbitration (mandative subjunctive or should).

watch.wrong: The suspect is said having fled the country.
watch.right: The suspect is said to have fled the country.
watch.why: After is said/believed/alleged comes to + infinitive (perfect if the event is earlier).

watch.wrong: The case is investigating by the police.
watch.right: The case is being investigated by the police.
watch.why: Ongoing process in the passive: is being + past participle.

watch.wrong: He was suggested to settle out of court.
watch.right: It was suggested that he settle out of court.
watch.why: Suggest does not take person + to; use it + that-clause.

watch.wrong: The director is believed that he forged the documents.
watch.right: The director is believed to have forged the documents.
watch.why: Or else: It is believed that the director forged…; the two structures are not mixed.

learn.title: Obligation, permission and responsibility in formal register
learn.html:
Contracts, regulations and rulings encode obligations and rights with very precise modal and prepositional vocabulary. A wrong preposition or modal can change the legal meaning.

FunctionExpressionEjemplo
Obligation (contractual)shall, is/are to, be required / obliged / bound toThe tenant shall pay rent monthly. Applications are to be submitted in writing.
Prohibitionmust not / shall not / may not, be prohibited fromTenants may not sublet the property without written consent.
Absence of obligationneedn't / don't have to / is not required toYou needn't resubmit the form.
Derechobe entitled to + noun / verbThe buyer is entitled to a full refund.
Responsabilidadbe liable for, be responsible for, be accountable to (someone) for (something)Directors can be held liable for losses caused by negligence.
Bindingbe bound by, be subject toAll parties are bound by the terms of the agreement.
Salvedadnotwithstanding, subject to, save for, except as providedNotwithstanding the foregoing, the supplier remains liable for latent defects.
  • Shall in legal English does not express the future, but obligation or instruction (The Company shall indemnify…). In everyday English it survives mostly in Shall we…?
  • Mustn't prohibits; needn't / don't have to indicate that there is no obligation. The Spanish “no debes” has only one meaning, which is why the mistake you don't must is so common.
  • Notwithstanding is a formal preposition/connector: notwithstanding the delay, or it can go after: the delay notwithstanding. Does not exist notwithstanding of.

watch.wrong: Participants mustn't to disclose the terms.
The buyer is entitled of a refund.
watch.right: The buyer is entitled to a refund.

watch.wrong: The company is responsible of any damage.
watch.right: The company is responsible for any damage.
watch.why: Responsible/liable for: the preposition is for, not of.

watch.wrong: You don't must disclose confidential data.
watch.why: To prohibit: mustn't. “Don't have to” only expresses absence of obligation.

learn.title: Formulas for negotiating and arguing precisely
learn.html:
• I would be prepared to … provided that … — offering a conditional concession: I would be prepared to extend the deadline, provided that payment is made in full.
  • Were you to accept …, we would be willing to … — proposing an exchange tentatively and politely.
  • Should this prove unacceptable, … — anticipating a refusal without dramatising it.
  • We are not in a position to … — rejecting firmly and without aggression: We are not in a position to waive the penalty.
  • I take your point, but … / With respect, … — disagreeing politely; with respect often signals a strong disagreement.
  • That said, … / Having said that, … — qualifying what has just been conceded.
  • Let me put it differently. — rephrasing to avoid a misunderstanding.
  • Subject to … / On the understanding that … — making an agreement conditional on a prior requirement.
  • Without prejudice to … — “without prejudice to…”: not giving up a right while making a concession.
  • In the interests of fairness, … — introducing a demand for fairness.

write.prompt: Write an essay of 300 to 400 words: “Should the law prioritise fairness over consistency?” Present two positions, concede at least one point to the opposing view and argue for your own conclusion. Use at least two formal conditionals (Were it not for / Had … / Should … / But for), three complex passives (is alleged to have, is being, must be seen to be) and the legal and ethical vocabulary from the unit.
checklist: At least two correct formal conditionals (Were it not for / Had it not been for / Should you… / But for + noun)
Three complex passives (to have been, being + past participle, modal + be)
At least 6 words from the unit's vocabulary (liability, precedent, accountable, impartial…)
One point conceded to the opposing view (I concede that… / admittedly)
Clear structure: introduction, two positions, conclusion
Formal register with no colloquial contractions
Between 300 and 400 words
write.model:
Should the law prioritise fairness over consistency? The question is as old as jurisprudence itself, and the answer is less obvious than either camp supposes.

The case for consistency is, at first sight, compelling. A legal system that treats like cases alike gives citizens predictability: they can plan their affairs, knowing that precedent will be respected and that no judge is free to decide according to personal preference. Were it not for this principle, the law would become arbitrary, and its authority would depend on the character of whoever happens to preside. Justice must not only be done but must be seen to be done, and it cannot be seen to be done if outcomes cannot be anticipated. Moreover, a judge who is alleged to have departed from established rules in order to reach a more congenial result is, rightly, held accountable.

The case for fairness is equally serious. Rules are written in general terms, yet cases are particular, and a rigid application of precedent can yield results that no reasonable person would call just. Had the courts of earlier centuries not been willing to soften harsh rules through equity, the law of contract would still be trapped in formalities that defeated the very bargains it was meant to protect. Fairness, on this view, is not the enemy of the law but its purpose, and consistency is merely its method.

I concede that the second position carries risk. Admittedly, a judge who is permitted to override rules for the sake of fairness acquires considerable power, and the impartiality of the system may be compromised. It is also true that fairness is a contested value; what seems fair to a claimant may seem entirely unjust to a defendant.

Nevertheless, I conclude that fairness should prevail where the two genuinely conflict, provided that the departure is exceptional, openly reasoned and subject to appeal. Such decisions are being scrutinised more closely in modern systems, and they must be seen to be grounded in principle rather than sympathy. But for such safeguards, I would favour consistency without reservation. With them, the law can remain predictable in the ordinary case and humane in the extraordinary one. Liability should follow responsibility, not mere technicality.

write.model:
Subject: Noise, service charges and repairs at Willow Court

Dear Mr Patel,

I am writing on behalf of the residents of Willow Court regarding three matters that have remained unresolved for several months: excessive noise from the ground-floor unit, an increase in service charges, and outstanding repairs to the communal areas. We hope that they can be settled amicably.

First, the noise. Since March, residents have been disturbed on most evenings by music from the commercial tenant, which continues well beyond the hours stipulated in the lease. Second, the service charges were raised by eighteen per cent in January without any itemised explanation. We are not in a position to accept an increase of this kind unless it is justified in writing. Third, the lift has been out of order for seven weeks, and the water damage in the stairwell has not been repaired, although both were reported in the spring.

The owners are bound by their obligations to maintain the common parts, and they may be held liable for the consequences of prolonged neglect. Residents are entitled to a quiet and safe environment, and several of us are considering whether we are obliged to withhold part of the charges.

Our proposal is as follows. I would be prepared to recommend that residents continue to pay the current charges, provided that you agree to three conditions: the noise is to be curbed by 10 p.m.; an itemised account is supplied within thirty days; and a timetable for repairs is confirmed in writing. Should you wish to discuss any of these points, I would welcome a meeting at your earliest convenience. Were you to accept, we would regard the matter as closed, without prejudice to our right to raise any new issue.

If, however, no satisfactory reply is received by the end of the month, the residents will have no option but to refer the matter to the housing ombudsman, and the repairs will be reported to the local authority. We would much prefer to avoid that course.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours sincerely,

Maria Santos
On behalf of the residents of Willow Court

reading.title: Justice by algorithm?
reading.intro: Read the opinion article and answer. Notice how the author concedes and refutes.
paragraphs: When a judge in a crowded courtroom decides how long a person should spend behind bars, the decision is supposed to rest on law, evidence and a measure of human judgment. Increasingly, however, it also rests on a number. In a growing number of jurisdictions, sentencing and bail hearings are informed by risk-assessment software that predicts, on the basis of a defendant's age, record and circumstances, how likely that person is to reoffend. Supporters regard these tools as a long-overdue corrective to the whims of individual judges; critics see in them a quiet revolution that has never been properly debated.

The case for the software is easily stated. Human beings are inconsistent. Studies of sentencing have repeatedly shown that two defendants convicted of near-identical offences can receive very different penalties, depending on the judge, the time of day or even the weather. Were it not for such arbitrariness, the argument goes, nobody would have thought of handing the task to a machine. An algorithm, by contrast, applies the same formula to everybody, and its reasoning can, in principle at least, be inspected, audited and corrected.

Yet the objection is equally serious. These models are trained on historical data, and historical data are the product of historical policing. If a neighbourhood has been patrolled heavily for decades, its residents will have been arrested more often, and a system that learns from those arrests will conclude that they are riskier. Bias is thus not eliminated but laundered: it re-enters the courtroom wearing the respectable clothing of mathematics. A widely cited investigation alleged that one popular tool wrongly labelled members of one ethnic group as high-risk far more often than others. The developers disputed the finding on technical grounds, and tellingly, statisticians have never fully settled the quarrel, because there are several mathematically incompatible definitions of fairness.

A second difficulty concerns transparency. Many of these systems are proprietary, and their makers argue that disclosing the formula would reveal trade secrets. But a defendant who is sentenced on the strength of a score he cannot examine is, in effect, denied the chance to rebut the case against him. Due process requires not merely that justice be done, but that it be seen to be done; a verdict that rests on a black box fails the second test, however accurate it may prove to be.

Defenders of the technology reply that nobody is proposing that machines should decide. The scores are advisory, they say, and the final word remains with the judge. This is reassuring only if judges actually behave that way. Research on automation bias suggests otherwise: people who are handed a confident-looking number tend to anchor on it, and departing from it requires a justification that deferring to it does not. Should a judge release a defendant whom the software rates as dangerous, and should that defendant go on to commit a crime, the judge will be held accountable in a way she would not have been had she followed the recommendation. The incentives, in other words, quietly push towards obedience.

What, then, should be done? A blanket ban seems unwise; some tools, carefully designed, may well outperform unaided intuition. But a number of safeguards are widely regarded as the minimum. Defendants should be entitled to know which factors were weighed, and to challenge them. Independent bodies should be empowered to audit the models regularly, and the results should be published. And, perhaps most importantly, there should be clarity about what the tools are for: to assist deliberation, not to replace it. Provided that those conditions are met, algorithmic assistance might well make courts fairer. Unless they are, we risk building a system that is efficient, consistent and, in the deepest sense, unaccountable.

listening.title: A mediation session
listening.intro: Listen to the mediation session between a tenant and her landlord. You can replay it.

lines.text: Good morning, both. Before we begin, let me remind you that this session is confidential, and that nothing said here can be used in court should the matter go that far.
Understood. Though I'll say at the outset that I think this is a waste of time. The lease is perfectly clear.
The lease is clear, Mr Brandt. What isn't clear is why my deposit was withheld when the damp was there before I moved in.
Because the damage was caused by condensation, which is the tenant's responsibility. Had you ventilated the flat properly, none of this would have happened.
I ventilated it every day. But for the broken extractor fan, which I reported in writing in October, there wouldn't have been any problem at all.
Mr Brandt, do you have a record of that report?
I do. I'll admit it was received. I just didn't consider it urgent.
That's a significant point. Ms Nair, supposing the deposit were returned in part, what would be an acceptable figure?
I'd be prepared to accept eighty per cent, provided that the landlord puts the repairs in writing and carries them out within a month.
Eighty is too much. Seventy, and I'll agree to the repairs, but I won't have a deadline imposed on me.
Might I suggest a compromise? Seventy-five per cent, and the repairs to be completed within six weeks, unless supplies are delayed.
Six weeks is a stretch, but I'm willing to meet you halfway, so long as the deadline is binding.
Fine. Should the work overrun, I'll cover the difference in rent for the extra days. But I won't go a penny further.
Then I think we have the outline of an agreement. I'll draft it, and you'll each have forty-eight hours to review it before signing.
